growth-policy-s1.title: Four programs in Navar (invented country)
growth-policy-s1.text:
The government of Navar, an invented country, is choosing among four programs of about the same cost:

  1. a tax credit for firms that buy new equipment;
  2. grants that pay for apprenticeships in skilled trades;
  3. a one-time cash payment to every household;
  4. funding for university research on cheaper batteries.

growth-policy-s2.title: Schooling, investment and growth in four invented countries

table.caption: Averages over 20 years in four invented countries
cols: Growth of real GDP per capita (% a year)

items.q: Which program mainly raises AD in the short run without directly adding to Navar's productive capacity?
options: The tax credit for firms that buy new equipment
The apprenticeship grants
The battery research funding
The one-time cash payment to households

why.correct: Spending that adds capital, skills or technology can shift LRAS; a cash transfer shifts AD.
options: Equipment is physical capital, which raises future capacity.
Apprenticeships build human capital, which raises what workers can produce.
Research can improve technology, which raises capacity.
Right: the payment raises disposable income and consumption (AD), but it adds no capital, skills or technology.

items.q: Through which channel do the apprenticeship grants promote growth?
options: More human capital: workers gain skills that raise productivity
More physical capital: firms buy more machines
Higher AD: apprentices spend the wages they earn, which shifts AD right
A lower price level: skilled workers accept lower wages

why.correct: Human capital channel: education and training raise output per worker.
options: Right: training and education build human capital.
That is the equipment tax credit's channel.
Their spending raises AD in the short run, but growth comes from their higher productivity.
The growth channel is what workers can produce, not their wages.

items.q: Which of these policies aim to shift Navar's LRAS to the right? Select all that apply.
options: The tax credit for new equipment
The apprenticeship grants
The one-time cash payment to households
The battery research funding
A new tax on business investment
A cut in funding for public universities

why.correct: Policies aimed at physical capital, human capital and technology aim at LRAS.
options: Right: it encourages investment in physical capital.
Right: they build human capital.
It raises spending (AD), not capacity.
Right: it aims at better technology.
Taxing investment discourages building physical capital, which works against LRAS.
Less funding for higher education works against human capital and research.

items.q: Navar is at full employment and pays for the programs by borrowing. Which effect could reduce the growth they produce?
options: Lower real interest rates that encourage too much private saving
Higher real interest rates that crowd out private investment
A fall in the price level that lowers nominal GDP
A rightward shift of SRAS that lowers output

why.correct: Deficit-financed growth programs can be partly offset by crowding out.
options: Government borrowing raises real rates, it does not lower them.
Right: more government borrowing raises the demand for loanable funds and the real rate, so private investment, and the capital it adds, falls.
Extra spending at full employment tends to raise the price level.
A rightward SRAS shift raises output; borrowing works through interest rates.

items.q: Compare Mera and Lith, which have the same investment share. What do the data suggest?
options: More investment is associated with faster growth
Schooling has no link to growth
More schooling goes with faster growth of real GDP per capita
Lith grew faster than Mera because it spent much less on schooling

why.correct: Holding investment fixed, the pair isolates schooling, a measure of human capital. With invented data and four countries, it is a pattern, not proof.
options: Investment is the same in Mera and Lith, so this pair cannot show its effect.
Mera, with more schooling, grew faster than Lith.
Right: with investment the same, Mera's extra schooling goes with 1 point faster growth.
Lith grew more slowly: 1.0 percent against Mera's 2.0 percent.

items.q: Which pair of countries best shows the link between physical capital and growth?
options: Mera and Lith
Nolo and Lith
Kova and Lith
Mera and Nolo

why.correct: To see one factor, compare countries that differ only in that factor.
options: They differ in schooling, not investment.
Right: they have the same schooling, and Nolo's higher investment goes with faster growth.
They differ in both schooling and investment, so the effects are mixed together.
They differ in both, and their growth rates are equal.

items.q: Lith wants to grow more like Kova. Which pair of policies fits the data?
options: Expand schooling and give firms incentives to invest in equipment
Raise taxes on investment and cut school funding to balance the budget
Send each household a cash payment each year
Raise the money supply faster to raise spending

why.correct: Growth policy aims at the sources of growth: human capital, physical capital and technology.
options: Right: Kova leads Lith in both schooling and investment.
Both would move Lith further from Kova.
Cash transfers raise AD; they do not build human or physical capital.
Faster money growth raises inflation in the long run, not capacity.

items.q: Kova's real GDP per capita is 20,000 dollars this year and grows at its table rate. What will it be next year, in dollars?

mistakes.why: You added 3 dollars. Growth of 3 percent means 3 percent of 20,000, which is 600 dollars.
You multiplied by 3. A 3 percent rise multiplies by 1.03.

options: Central bank actions that change the supply of money
Changes in government spending meant to raise AD in a recession, with no aim at capacity
Tax and spending changes meant to raise incentives to work, save and invest, shifting LRAS right
Limits on how much firms may produce

why.correct: Supply-side policies target LRAS through incentives and investment.
options: That is monetary policy.
That is demand-side (stabilization) fiscal policy.
Right: supply-side policy aims at the economy's capacity, not just at spending.
Supply-side policy aims to raise production, not limit it.

items.q: A government cuts tax rates on wages and on business investment. What effects are expected in the short run and the long run?
options: Short run: AD shifts right. Long run: if work and investment rise, LRAS shifts right too
Short run: LRAS shifts left. Long run: AD shifts left
Short run: nothing changes. Long run: the price level falls
Short run: SRAS shifts left. Long run: the deficit closes the gap by itself

why.correct: Many policies work on both sides: AD in the short run, LRAS in the long run.
options: Right: lower taxes raise disposable income and spending now; stronger incentives to work and invest can raise capacity later. How large that second effect is remains debated.
Lower taxes raise spending and, if anything, capacity; neither curve shifts left.
Tax cuts raise disposable income right away, so AD shifts right in the short run.
A tax cut does not raise firms' costs, and a deficit does not close a gap by itself.

items.q: A government at full employment begins building a large network of highways. Show the short-run effect of the construction spending itself, and mark the new short-run equilibrium.

why.correct: Government spending is part of AD, so AD shifts right; in the short run real output and the price level rise.

slips.LRAS: The finished highways can raise capacity later; while they are being built, the spending shows up as higher AD.

items.q: Years later, the finished highways cut shipping times and costs for firms across the economy. Shift the curve that shows the long-run effect on productive capacity.

why.correct: Better infrastructure raises productivity, so potential output rises and LRAS shifts right.

slips.AD: The question asks about capacity once the highways are built; that is LRAS, not spending.

items.q: Stronger patent protection for new inventions is a policy aimed mainly at which source of growth?
options: Human capital
Technology
Natural resources
Aggregate demand

why.correct: Research funding and patents target technology.
options: Human capital is workers' skills and education.
Right: patents let inventors earn a return on new ideas, which encourages research and new methods.
Patents cover ideas, not land or minerals.
Patents work on the supply side, through innovation.

items.q: How can reducing government budget deficits promote long-run growth?
options: Smaller deficits raise AD, which raises potential output
Smaller deficits raise the money supply, which raises real output
Smaller deficits raise the price level, which raises nominal GDP
Less government borrowing lowers real interest rates, so private investment and the capital stock grow faster

why.correct: Deficit reduction can support growth by freeing saving for private investment.
options: Cutting a deficit lowers AD in the short run; the growth effect works through investment.
The budget does not set the money supply, and money is neutral in the long run.
Growth is about real capacity, not nominal values.
Right: smaller deficits reduce crowding out.

items.q: An economy at full employment raises transfer payments to households. What is the main effect, and on which curve?
options: AD shifts right: the price level rises, with little lasting output gain
LRAS shifts right, so potential output rises and the PPC shifts outward
SRAS shifts right, so the price level falls
AD shifts left, so output falls

why.correct: Policies that raise spending shift AD; only those that raise capacity shift LRAS.
options: Right: transfers raise disposable income and spending, but at full employment they mostly push up prices; they do not add capacity.
Transfers raise spending, not capital, skills or technology.
Transfers do not lower firms' costs.
More transfers raise spending, shifting AD right.

items.q: Build the chain from a job-training program to long-run growth.

why.correct: Training builds human capital, productivity rises, potential output rises, and LRAS shifts right.

specific.frame: The program trains workers, so ___ capital rises. Each worker can produce more, so productivity ___. Potential output rises, so ___ shifts right.
specific.model: The program trains workers, so human capital rises. Each worker can produce more, which means productivity rises. As a result potential output rises, so LRAS shifts right and the PPC shifts out.

concept.label: Which capital
options: human
physical

why.1: Training adds skills, which is human capital; physical capital is equipment.

change.label: Productivity
options: rises
falls

why.1: More skills mean more output per worker.

curve.label: Which curve shifts right
options: LRAS
AD

why.1: Higher capacity shifts LRAS; AD shows spending.
